title: Kyle
text:
Biography
My name is Kyle Suelflow, and I am a Senior at Macalester College majoring in Data Science with a minor in Environmental Studies. My core interest lies in data visualization. To be able to tell a story using data requires understanding of how viewers perceive color, shape, and size. The challenge of figuring out how to show data in an elegant yet understandable way is one that I enjoy tackling. I wish to utilize my skills in data visualization and analysis in data journalism, climate modeling, and sports analytics.

title: Kyle
text:
Personal
I love to go hiking and backpacking, having taken trips to Banff national park and Acadia national park this past summer. At Macalester College, I am the President of the Open Ultimate frisbee team, which takes up a lot of my time. Additionally, I play both club and professional ultimate frisbee in Minnesota, and this summer I competed with the U-24 USA mixed national team in Spain at the world championships! Outside of frisbee, I enjoy cooking and playing games. You can find me scrolling NYT cooking for ideas often. Some board games I like to play include Terraforming Mars, Settlers of Catan, and Rail Baron.

title: Blocks4All
text: In the summer of 2023 I helped to continue to develop Blocks4All. Blocks4All is an accessible block based programming IPad app aimed at students who are in elementary school. It is designed to work well for students with motor and visual impairments, using Switch Control and Voice Over to aid in their learning. I worked on some app development as well as website development (linked here). We used Swift and UiKit to construct the app, and used HTML, CSS, and Javascript for the website. Learning all these languages was a fun and challenging process.

title: Time Series Solar Analysis
text:
Unable to display PDF file. Download instead.
In this capstone project from STAT 452, Correlated Data, my partner and I modeled global horizontal irradiance, or GHI, in 3 different locations around the world. These are Seychelles, Kenya, and England. Kenya and Seychelles are at similar latitudes but different climates, and Manchester, England is significantly more northern, providing a completely different set of data. We used modeling techniques from both time series and longitudinal to model GHI across 25 years of data. Specifically, we modeled intra-day variation and seasonal variation.

title: Rail Baron Analysis
text:
Unable to display PDF file. Download instead.
The above image shows Rail Baron, a classic board game where the objective is to move from city to city as cheaply as possible. The easiest way to do this is to buy railroads, and utilize them for free. The image shows the optimal set of 6 railroads that build the best network. All the railroads are listed on the edge of the gameboard, along with their ranking of importance. We depicted the game board as a graph, where each node represents a different rail road. Nodes are connected if railroads connect to eachother. More information on our methodology can be found in our paper above, in sections 2 and 3. This project was for Computational Linear Algebra at Macalester College.

title: Solar and Wind Energy in the US
text: In this project, my partner and I’s goal was to investigate the potential for solar and wind energy in the United States. We fit linear models to some summary measures of solar and wind use, to determine which states doing better or worse than they should have been. Additionally, I created some gifs of wind and solar potential in the US. The wind gif is shown above, where the altitude at which the wind speed is measured is changing. This was a fun challenge, working with mapping and animation packages in R to create a fascinating map. This project was for Intermediate Data Science.

title: Age Heaping in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: Throughout the last 2 years, I have been working with Taylor Okonek to investigate the impact that age heaping has on several different techniques that model under-five mortality rate. Age heaping refers to the artificial spike of deaths amongst children at 12 months, where there is a relatively large amount of deaths compared to surrounding ages. These deaths are recorded via surveys, as in many low and middle income countries, there is poor registration systems. We simulate children’s deaths in order to control the amount of age heaping that occurs. This project has been very rewarding in many ways, helping me gain valuable skills using parallel programming and simulation techniques. Most of all, I hope that are work can be used to help make more accurate estimations of child mortality in low and middle income countries.
